key_facts: The prototype is designed with a curved shape resembling a banana.
The prototype features a bright yellow color scheme mandated by the company.
The primary control mechanism of the remote is a scroll wheel.
The prototype includes rubber grips to address the user requirement for a spongy feel.
The team evaluates the prototype based on criteria derived from previous user complaints.
The team assigns a score of one to the prototype for simplicity and intuitiveness.
The team decides to incorporate a proximity alarm feature to address the issue of lost remotes.
The team assigns a score of four for technological innovation because the technology is derived from the iPod.
The average evaluation score calculated for the prototype is 2.42.
The project has a strict production cost budget of 12.50 Euros per unit.
The initial prototype configuration, including an LCD display, exceeds the budget with a cost of 15.50 Euros.
The team decides to remove the LCD display component to reduce production costs.
The final design relies on the television screen for interface feedback instead of a built-in remote screen.
The final adjusted production cost of the remote meets the budget target of 12.50 Euros.
The remote is powered by two batteries to avoid excessive weight.
The remote utilizes an advanced chip-on-print and a double-curved plastic case.

key_facts: Grad D is organizing a blind tiramisu tasting contest for the upcoming weekend.
The group conducted a wizard-of-oz test on Friday with Litonya serving as the first subject.
The reading portion of the wizard test took five minutes, which the group determined was too long.
The test subject, Litonya, did not follow the intended order of the bullet points during the reading task.
Fey suggested that the system should introduce itself when called to improve the wizard introduction.
Liz suggested switching tasks between the computer and the human wizard for different subjects to gather better data.
Professor B agrees that the group should hire Fey and pay her for the time she has put into the project.
Professor B suggests that Fey could take on the job of organizing test subjects.
Professor B signed the group up for a presentation slot on Wednesday to discuss system design with computer scientists and linguists.
Grad A created a pedagogical belief-net based on image schemas like Trajector-Landmark and Source-Path-Goal.
The bottom layer of Grad A's belief-net represents the "Mode," which is the decision variable.
Professor B is concerned that Grad A's current belief-net structure could lead to a combinatorial explosion of inputs to the Mode node.
Professor B suggests using technical methods like Noisy-ORs or knowledge engineering tricks to narrow nodes to manage belief-net complexity.
Grad D integrated a rule into the SmartKom system where a "Landmark" object type triggers a "Vista" action.
Grad D proposes replacing hard-coded rules in the system with a belief-net to decide which construction to activate.
Professor B wants the system to use deep cognitive linguistics to create generalizations that allow mechanism re-use across different tasks.
The group agrees to hold future meetings in the current location to utilize the display equipment.

I'm pleased to report that our progress remains on track for additional dry van production to begin in early 2023.
As we discuss these capacity changes with the investment community over the last quarter, I'd like to read those at a few points that I believe are helpful in explaining our rationale for these changes and the forthcoming benefits.
Going to market as One Wabash allows a portfolio selling approach that leverages the unrivaled breadth of our products.
That capability to meet this new customer demand more fully for our flagship dry van product is tremendously important in supporting our portfolio selling approach.
Additionally, our enhanced dry van capacity will allow us to more adequately supply product to our Wabash exclusive and industry-leading dealer network.
This added capacity is also necessary to supply logistics market that continues to drive changes in the way trailers are utilized.
Drop and hook is a strategy carriers use to maximize drivers' time on the road.
Driver shortages are a persistent problem but have become more severe since 2020 with little clarity on how or when this situation will materially improve.
Overall, our customers' incremental economics of adding a trailer to a tractor have meaningfully increased and represent a compelling value proposition in the marketplace.
Additionally, incremental demand for dry van trailers is being generated by customers that did not consume trailer supply to 10 years ago.
Private fleet and freight brokers are building trailer pools to ensure consistent access to capacity and more effectively leverage our only capacity.
Given our efforts to grow dry van production, we have also planned several steps ahead to ensure stability of component supply.
As 1 example, our management team has spent time with our supply partners at Hydro, a global leader in aluminum extrusions which have historically been in high demand during times of elevated trailer industry build rates.
The Hydro team appreciates the vision that Wabash is working to bring to life and Hydro has agreed to be a key supplier for Wabash over the life of a 10-year supply agreement which is a meaningful development, increasing supply certainty for both our existing and new dry van capacity.
When considering the differentiation facilitated by our industry-leading lightweight panel technology, we believe this capacity expansion creates an incredible long-term opportunity for Wabash.
We also remain on track with our plan to scale our innovative molded structural composite technology within refrigerated vans, truck bodies and other transportation logistics and distribution-related products.
We believe we have a unique technology and operational capability that has the ability to disrupt the broad Cold Chain product market as well as change operating models for carriers and shippers.
These composite technologies facilitate improved operating efficiency for our customers, changes the model of asset usage and life while also supporting a customer base that is increasingly focused on sustainability and reducing their carbon footprint.
We now have over 25 million miles logged to date and we are excited to scale this opportunity as we move into full commercialization of this product technology.
Finally, we believe long-term investors will be rewarded in the near term by our dry van capacity project as our converted traditional refrigerated van facility will produce 10,000 units post conversion which is twice as many dry vans as compared to the reefers that were previously manufactured.
Notably, dry vans carry a higher margin compared with our conventional refrigerated product.
All told, we expect to realize $0.15 to $0.20 of annual earnings per share accretion in 2023 and beyond as a result of this near-term capacity move.
This capacity project will also enable us to further create shareholder value as we fully commercialize our breakthrough all composite refrigerated technology over the next several years.
Moving to market conditions; demand for freight remains robust and supply continues to be constrained by a multitude of factors, strong business investment and consumer spending paired with persistently low inventory levels continue to propagate robust levels of freight activity.
We see the overall freight environment remaining positive through 2022 and well into 2023.
Coupled with structural changes, as previously discussed, in terms of e-commerce related logistics disruption, the entry of new customers and the emergence of large trailer pools, we see demand remaining robust for an extended period of time, possibly the strongest period of demand we have seen in history.
As a reminder, the trailer industry has a strong seasonal pattern of ordering activity in which OEM backlogs built during the second half of the calendar year.
The strength within our customer businesses from First to Final Mile has been well reflected in our backlog which increased by $600 million sequentially in Q3 to a total of $1.9 billion.
This represents an 87% increase versus the same period last year.
$1.9 billion in backlog also establishes a new record for our order book which is a testament to our new commercial structure and market strength as well as changing dynamics of how the market utilizes trailers.
The strength in our backlog creates the visibility necessary to offer an initial earnings per share outlook for 2022 $1.70, assuming no improvement in supply chain conditions.
In closing, we're excited to announce our identity change and the realignment of our external reporting with our operating structure, our growth initiatives and our strategy going forward.
Our portfolio of transportation solutions positions us to leverage unmatched product breadth as a competitive advantage, shored up by unified commercial structure and go-to-market strategy.
We expect our increased dry van capacity to be a linchpin to many new and expanded customer relationships and our shift to all composite refrigerated technology to drive growth well into the future.
Driving focus in our parts and service business enhances visibility to our higher margin, more repeatable business that features ample potential for growth.
These reporting changes are the culmination of modifications to our organization.
to facilitate our refreshed strategy and we're eager to share our progress with you as the new reporting structure enables more effective communication.
We believe a story that started with a change in vision and a deep desire by so many of Wabash to be different, to be better.
Ultimately, we are living our purpose with action to change how the world reaches you.
With that, I'll hand it over to Mike for his comments.
I'd like to start by offering some brief thoughts on the announcement Brent just discussed.
Following our strategic, organizational and capacity update, today's company branding and segmentation refreshes are the culmination of work that has been going on behind the scenes for the last 2 years.
Our decision to narrow our strategic focus to transportation, logistics and distribution markets comes at a time of dramatic and exciting changes within the industry and we are tremendously excited with how the following moves have positioned us to leverage our commercial organization and innovation and product development capabilities to lead our markets forward.
Turning to a review of our third quarter financial results.
Consolidated third quarter revenue was $483 million with new trailer and truck body shipments of approximately 12,455 units and 3,780 units, respectively.
Gross margin was 10.6% of sales during the quarter, while operating margin came in at 3.8%.
Operating EBITDA for the third quarter was $33 million or 6.8% of sales.
Finally, for the quarter, net income was $11 million or $0.22 per diluted share.
From a segment perspective, Transportation Solutions generated revenue of $443 million and operating income of $26 million.
Parts and Service generated revenue of $42 million and operating income of $4.1 million.
Year-to-date operating cash flow was negative $74 million.
Shipments that were skewed very late in the quarter caused our receivables to increase significantly from Q2.
We have also increased inventory in certain areas of our business to help buffer supply chain interruptions.
We would expect Q4 to have a significant amount of free cash generation.
Our current target for 2021 capital spending is approximately $50 million which is higher than normal as we catch up on projects that were deferred during COVID and prepared for our strategic capacity expansion and the conversion of our Laveya-base south plant from reefer capacity to drive an capacity.
With regard to our balance sheet, our liquidity or cash plus available borrowings as of September 30 was $259 million with $49 million of cash and cash equivalents and approximately $220 million of availability on our revolving credit facility.
In late September and early October, we upsized our revolving credit facility by $50 million to $225 million and closed an issuance of $400 million in senior notes, respectively.
After repaying our previous senior notes and term loan, our improved debt structure will result in $3 million of annual interest expense savings and more importantly, create a reasonably priced patient debt structure that allows us to invest in our business and enhances our opportunities to create value with a lower cost of capital.
With regard to capital allocation during the third quarter, we utilized $14 million to repurchase shares and our quarterly dividend of $4 million and invested $9 million in capital projects.
Our capital allocation focus continues to prioritize reinvestment in the business through growth CapEx while also maintaining our dividend and evaluate opportunities for share repurchase alongside bolt-on M&A opportunities.
Thinking about the next 3 to 5 years, I expect our capital allocation to continue to support our internal opportunities for organic growth.
We have exciting opportunities to generate rates of return well in excess of our cost of capital as we progress with initiatives on our Transportation Solutions and Parts and Services segment.
Our dividend also remains an important element of returning capital to shareholders.
Given that we expect our future free cash flow profile to remain robust, we will continue to provide an opportunity to repurchase shares when we consider that to the under value.
While we will continue to evaluate smaller acquisition opportunities that would easily fold into our existing operations, I believe any large deal will be a lesser priority compared to the internal opportunities we have in front of us.
Moving on to our outlook for 2021.
We do expect Q4 to represent peak pain for estimate margin perspective.
This will be the quarter while the price cost most heavily works against us as we produce for orders that were booked in late 2020, after which material costs have run substantially.
We expect revenue in the range of $490 million to $520 million and earnings per share of $0.10 to $0.15 for the quarter.
As Brent mentioned, our record backlog allows us to offer an initial outlook for 2022 of $1.70 per share.
I'd like to be clear about the assumptions behind our 2022 outlook.
Pricing recovery from commodity headwinds experienced in 2021 have been effective and we expect average selling prices for trailers to increase in the range of $5,000 to $6,000 year-over-year.
This would represent a $0.60 tailwind in the bridge from our anticipated $0.52 of earnings per share in 2021 to our guide of $1.70 in 2022.
I'd like to emphasize a modification to our pricing construct for 2022, where we have implemented pass-through commodity pricing with many trailer customers.
We have targeted a certain margin and have agreed to pass through commodity costs.
We feel this provides more certainty around our forward financial expectations and we hope to continue with this framework in future years.
We're also assuming over $0.90 from improved build rates which are based on the ramp in factory floor associate count we've been able to achieve to date.
We expect to gain a total of $0.10 from the combination of reduced year-over-year share count as well as lower interest expense.
Fixed overhead and SG&A will partially offset the significant gains as a result of the impact from the current inflationary environment.
We are assuming no improvement in supply chain in our guidance.
Clearly, we hope that as time goes on, the supply chain situation improves but we're not building that level of optimism into our outlook.
However, this clearly would provide upside opportunity should the present state of supply chain improve.
Operating margins are expected to be approximately 6% at the midpoint and we are well on our way to achieving our 8% operating margin target by 2023.
We are excited about our opportunity to meaningfully expand the company's profitability and earnings per share year-over-year and about the strong underpinning of the demand for our products driven by both strong demand conditions and structural changes in the market.
In conclusion, the announcements we've made today are the culmination of work that has been going on behind the scenes for the last 3 years.
Our strategic focus is well set to leverage the company's strength as our organizational structure improvements proactively position us to drive innovation at a time when the market most needs it.
Additionally, while our new segment structure provides visibility to our important parts and service business, I'd like to reinforce that our parts and services team is working on initiatives meant to holistically benefit Wabash which means we're thoroughly flowing through the lifetime value of our equipment for customers, further enhancing Wabash's value to our industry-leading dealer network and effectively leveraging our carefully curated supplier partnerships.
We are building something exciting by filling in the white space around our traditional first to final mile portfolio of transportation solutions.
All told, nearing our strategy to focus on transportation, logistics and distribution restructuring our organization around these customers and going to market as One Wabash to most effectively leverage the breadth of our portfolio of solutions as building a new identity for our company.
This new identity is underlined by the modification of our company's name.
Our ticker will remain WNC but Wabash will stand for changing how the world reaches you.

key_facts: Visitors from DFKI, part of the German SmartKom project, visited the research group the previous week.
The SmartKom system can now process speech input and respond using a German synthesis module for English sentences.
The SmartKom system utilizes a concept-to-speech approach rather than simple text-to-speech.
Johno (Grad D) wrote tree-adjoining grammars for several sentences within the SmartKom system.
The SmartKom system's knowledge base is formatted in a LISP-like form.
The SmartKom system's syntactic structure builder is based on Prolog.
The SmartKom system was originally designed to work with a Siemens virtual touch screen.
The research group plans to shift focus from the applied SmartKom demo to basic scientific issues during the summer.
Keith (Grad B) is tasked with working on English and German constructions for the domain during the summer.
Bhaskara is leaving the project on June 1st.
Bhaskara will provide a running belief net for the subdomain before his departure.
Grad G and Grad E are tasked with finalizing the belief net design by the following Monday.
JavaBayes software does not support the node explosion visualization required for the belief net.
Grad E will send transcribed English and German data from trial runs to Keith (Grad B).
Professor C cited research indicating that separate brain areas process objects within reach versus objects out of reach.
A new doctoral student named Eva will join the project in August.
Nancy, Johno (Grad D), and Professor C plan to collaborate on parser development.
The group aims to utilize the same construction analyzer for both the applied SmartKom project and Nancy's child language modeling.
Ami (PhD A) plans to travel to Switzerland in June or July for consulting.
Robert needs to select a specific topic for his absentee thesis.

key_facts: The Meeting Recorder project aims to collect data for research on meeting information retrieval.
Participants in the meeting must read digit strings individually to establish ground truth for the audio recordings.
Participants are required to sign a consent form and a speaker form.
Meeting transcripts will be anonymized, but the audio recordings will not be anonymized.
Grad B proposes a research task to infer user intentions in a tourist navigation domain.
The three specific user intentions identified for the research task are Vista, Enter, and Tango.
The Vista intention refers to a user wanting to view an object.
The Enter intention refers to a user wanting to go inside a building.
The Tango intention refers to a user wanting to touch or get very close to an object.
Current GIS systems often route users to the closest geometric point rather than the appropriate entrance or viewpoint.
The research group plans to use a Belief Network to distinguish between the Vista, Enter, and Tango intentions.
Inputs for the proposed Belief Network will include linguistic cues, situational context, and object ontology.
The SmartKom system's current parser output is insufficient for distinguishing specific user intentions.
Grad E and Grad F are assigned to select a Belief Network software package.
Grad E and Grad F are expected to present their selected Belief Network package the following Monday.
The group plans to conduct a data collection experiment using a Wizard of Oz setup.
Fey Parrill is a candidate to act as the Wizard for the data collection experiment.
Grad B received the NT and Linux versions of the navigation system software.
The Linux version of the software failed to unpack due to a timestamp error involving a future date.
Data exchange between the system modules will be handled using XML.

key_facts: The research group is discussing data collection strategies for the Meeting Recorder project.
The research group decides to use CrossPads in a pilot study to track note-taking activity during meetings.
The research group agrees to collect electronic meeting minutes and record oral summaries from participants to aid in query generation.
The research group decides to take digital photographs of meeting whiteboards and seating arrangements to preserve context.
The research group plans to send recorded meeting data on CD-ROMs to IBM for transcription.
Professor A will email James Landay to request CrossPads and text sources for the project.
Professor C requests that group members recruit non-technical users to test the Communicator dialogue system.
Professor A plans to install eight-channel digital recording equipment at the University of Washington by early August.
The research group decides to record various meeting types to capture natural speech overlap rather than enforcing strict interaction rules.
The research group identifies the automatic generation of search queries from meeting summaries as a significant research challenge.

key_facts: Council Bill 245 proposes rezoning the property at 2423-2490 South University Boulevard from G-MX-3 to G-RX-5.
The current G-MX-3 zoning allows for three-story mixed-use buildings with a maximum height of 45 feet.
The proposed G-RX-5 zoning allows for five-story residential mixed-use buildings with a maximum height of 70 feet.
The applicant for the rezoning is Node Colorado.
Node Colorado has assembled ownership of the majority of the block at 2423-2490 South University Boulevard.
A valid petition of protest filed by the neighborhood required a supermajority of ten affirmative votes for Council Bill 245 to pass.
The Denver Planning Board voted 9 to 0 to recommend support of the rezoning application.
The University Park Community Council voted 11 to 0 to oppose the rezoning application.
Community Planning and Development staff recommended approval of Council Bill 245 based on consistency with adopted plans.
The University Park Neighborhood Plan designates the site as part of the Ivy Towers district.
The University Park Neighborhood Plan recommends moderate densities of 3 to 5 stories for the Ivy Towers district.
The proposed development concept includes approximately 230 to 240 rental units and 25,000 square feet of retail space.
The developer plans to construct underground parking to accommodate the proposed density.
Opponents of Council Bill 245 cited concerns regarding increased traffic congestion on University Boulevard and adjacent neighborhood streets.
Opponents argued that the 2010 zoning update established appropriate three-story limits for the site and that conditions have not changed sufficiently to warrant rezoning.
The University of Denver expressed support for the proposed rezoning.
Councilman Charlie Brown supported Council Bill 245, citing its consistency with the 2008 University Park Neighborhood Plan.
Denver City Council passed Council Bill 245 with 13 affirmative votes.

key_facts: Council Bill 760 proposes amendments to five overlapping plans in the 38th and Blake Station area.
The plan amendments aim to clarify building height visions and promote higher design quality near the 38th and Blake Station.
The 38th and Blake Station area amendments recommend taller building heights, up to 16 stories, near the station platform.
Access to increased building heights in the 38th and Blake Station area is conditional on the provision of community benefits.
The specific community benefits required for increased height include integrated affordable housing and higher design quality.
The plan amendments require height transitions from taller station-area buildings down to surrounding residential neighborhoods like Cole and Curtis Park.
The plan establishes 'base heights' derived from previously adopted plans and 'incentive heights' available through community benefits.
The amendments recommend a regulatory approach to design quality that includes mass reduction and screened parking.
The 38th and Blake Station area amendments establish the river corridor as an amenity that should be treated with the same design standards as a primary street.
The affordable housing component functions as a density bonus incentive rather than a penalty.
Implementation of the plan's recommendations will require future regulatory tools, such as a design overlay district.
Representatives from Curtis Park Neighbors and the RiNo Art District spoke in support of Council Bill 760.
Councilwoman Ortega raised concerns regarding train safety and the transport of hazardous materials adjacent to the proposed high-density development.
The 38th and Blake Station area steering committee did not specifically discuss train safety regarding flammable liquids during the planning process.
Council Bill 760 was passed by the Denver City Council.

key_facts: The Long Beach City Council considered a recommendation to authorize the City Manager to create a partnership program for the Parks, Recreation, and Marine Departments.
The proposed partnership program aims to enhance parks, programs, and services citywide.
The new program consolidates existing citywide sponsorship policies, fee waiver policies, and right of entry permits into a single framework.
The program was modeled after successful partnership programs in cities such as San Francisco, Minneapolis, Seattle, Kansas City, Sacramento, and New York.
The Parks, Recreation, and Marine Department currently manages over 100 existing partnerships.
Identified needs for the program fall into three categories: parks and facilities, additional programming, and expanded services.
Partnership opportunities under the new policy include donations, sponsorships, revenue sharing, volunteer support, and facility naming rights.
Guiding principles for the program require partnerships to bring new revenues or resources and meet a community need.
Partnerships must have a positive social, financial, cultural, or environmental impact.
Partnerships are required to protect and enhance the City of Long Beach's brand and image.
Partnerships must be self-sustaining and not require additional resources from the City of Long Beach.
The application process requires interested businesses or organizations to submit a letter of intent for review.
Friends of Long Beach Animals is partnering with the city to fund the construction of an expanded dog play yard.
The Heart of Ida organization provides free senior services in exchange for space at the Fourth Street Senior Center.
The Conservation Corps will serve as a subcontractor to assist community organizations with park enhancement projects.
The policy explicitly states that proposals seeking to assume delivery of existing programs will not be considered if they violate Proposition L.
Councilman Austin requested that the policy's guiding principles explicitly state that partnerships must follow existing labor agreements.
Director Marie Knight confirmed that the partnership policy includes medians, parkways, and roundabouts under the purview of Parks, Recreation, and Marine.
Revenue sharing for concessions or fundraising will be negotiated separately for each individual contract.
The policy incorporates the existing process where the Parks and Recreation Commission reviews and approves fee waiver requests based on community benefit.
Councilwoman Mungo requested that approved applications be scanned and posted on the city website for transparency.
Partners of Parks provides fiscal sponsorships and insurance certificates for community groups that do not have 501(c)(3) status.
The Arts Council for Long Beach supports the policy to help activate underused spaces like the East Village Arts Park.
Friends of El Dorado Dog Park supported the policy for providing clear guidelines regarding corporate sponsorship fundraising.

key_facts: Council Bill 247 concerns a rezoning request for a 0.6-acre property located at the northeast corner of Third Avenue and Knox Court in the Barnum neighborhood.
The subject property is currently zoned ESU-D1x, which is an urban edge single-unit residential district that allows for accessory dwelling units.
The rezoning request seeks to change the property's zoning to IMU-2.5 with a waiver to accommodate multi-unit residential development.
The requested waiver allows the apartment building form to reach 2.5 stories in the front 65 percent of the lot, exceeding the standard two-story cap for apartments in the IMU-2.5 district.
The subject site is currently a vacant surface parking lot and was historically used as a telephone service company garage.
City staff recommended approval of the rezoning, citing consistency with Comprehensive Plan 2040 and Blueprint Denver policies regarding infill development and housing diversity.
The Barnum Neighborhood Plan, adopted in 1986, contains policies supporting the preservation of low-density residential character as well as reinvestment at strategic locations.
The property owners, represented by Greg Osborn and Matthew Guarino, stated their intention to develop attainable housing for entry-level workers and first-time homebuyers.
The property owners confirmed that the project is privately funded and does not utilize public subsidies or Low Income Housing Tax Credits.
There is no binding legal agreement or covenant in place that compels the developers to build affordable or attainable housing on the site.
The proposed zoning requires a minimum of one vehicle parking space per residential unit.
City staff confirmed that parking reductions for micro-units are not permitted under the proposed zoning for this site.
Councilman Espinosa noted that the rezoning allows for both apartment and townhouse forms, which could potentially result in market-rate products rather than the discussed attainable housing.
Council Bill 247 passed the City Council with 12 ayes and 0 nays.

key_facts: The Marketing Expert identifies the product's look and feel as the most important customer requirement based on focus group results.
The Marketing Expert identifies technological innovation as the second most important customer requirement.
The Marketing Expert identifies ease of use as the third most important customer requirement.
The Marketing Expert proposes a design trend inspired by fruit and vegetables, featuring bright colors and a spongy texture.
The team discusses implementing changeable covers to allow users to customize the remote control's appearance.
The User Interface Designer proposes speech recognition functionality to store and recall channel names.
The User Interface Designer suggests that a limited vocabulary of 80 to 100 words is sufficient for the speech recognition feature.
The User Interface Designer proposes using an LCD display and toggle switch to manage multiple device modes.
The User Interface Designer suggests a blinking light feature to indicate battery status and help locate the remote in the dark.
The Project Manager enforces a production cost budget of 12.50 Euro per unit.
The Industrial Designer confirms that a single FPGA chip can support both scroll wheels and LCD functions.
The Project Manager instructs the design team to prepare two distinct prototype designs for the next meeting.
One requested prototype must be a basic, lower-cost version.
One requested prototype must be an advanced, higher-end version.
The team decides to use a standard plastic case for the base model of the remote control.
The Marketing Expert is tasked with preparing a method to evaluate the upcoming prototypes.

key_facts: Councilmember Richardson recommended authorizing the City Manager to negotiate an agreement with the City of Bellflower for a traffic study at the intersection of Downey Avenue and 64th Street.
Residents of the Ramona Park and Andy Street neighborhoods have reported long-standing issues with speeding and low visibility at the intersection of Downey Avenue and 64th Street.
The City of Bellflower stated they will allow a traffic study only if the City of Long Beach agrees to fund the entire construction cost of a traffic signal if one is warranted.
The estimated cost to install a traffic signal at the intersection of Downey Avenue and 64th Street ranges from $175,000 to $250,000.
Councilmember Richardson identified $175,000 from District 9 infrastructure funds to contribute toward the traffic signal project.
Approximately 75 percent of the intersection of Downey Avenue and 64th Street is located within the City of Bellflower.
